message:
QUESTION:
Which supplier, A or B, should the firm use for component K-220, given that a delivery taking longer than 26 days causes a stockout?

DATA:
Choosing a supplier for component K-220. Safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days. Any delivery that takes longer than 26 days causes a stockout, which halts the assembly line.

Last 12 orders from each supplier, lead time in days (order placed to goods received), in date order:
Supplier A (sea freight): 21, 23, 22, 24, 20, 22, 45, 23, 21, 22, 24, 21
Supplier B (road and rail): 18, 19, 30, 17, 29, 18, 31, 19, 28, 18, 30, 19

Notes:
- A's 45-day delivery was the order shipped in February, during the documented three-week national port strike, which delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since, and none is planned.
- B had no comparable disruption. B's deliveries of 28 days or more are spread throughout the year.
- Unit price: A £4.10, B £4.05. Annual volume about 40,000 units.
- Both suppliers meet the quality specification for K-220.
- This decision applies to K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts with different specifications, volumes and routes.

<analysis>
# Supplier Choice for K-220: Lead-Time Analysis (Revised)

**Recommendation: award the K-220 contract to Supplier A.** Our safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days, so the question that matters is how often each supplier goes past 26 days. In the last 12 orders, B went past 26 days five times, spread through the year. A went past it once, during a documented national port strike that has not recurred. B's 5p unit saving, about £2,000 a year, does not come close to covering the cost of repeated line stoppages.

## Objective and decision criterion

A delivery over 26 days causes a stockout and halts the assembly line. The criterion is therefore the **frequency of deliveries exceeding 26 days**, and whether those exceedances are likely to recur. Average lead time is a poor guide. A supplier can have a good average and still breach the threshold often, and a supplier with a slightly worse average can breach it almost never.

## Data

These are the last 12 orders from each supplier, in days from order placed to goods received.

- **Supplier A (sea):** 21, 23, 22, 24, 20, 22, **45**, 23, 21, 22, 24, 21
- **Supplier B (road/rail):** 18, 19, **30**, 17, **29**, 18, **31**, 19, **28**, 18, **30**, 19

Bold values exceed 26 days.

| | Supplier A | Supplier B |
|---|---|---|
| Mean lead time | 24.0 days | 23.0 days |
| Median lead time | 22 days | 19 days |
| Range | 20–45 days | 17–31 days |
| Orders over 26 days | **1 of 12** | **5 of 12 (42%)** |
| Cause of exceedances | February port strike (one-off, documented) | No identified disruption; spread through the year |
| Mean excluding A's strike order | 22.1 days (max 24) | n/a |

*Correction to the earlier draft: B's mean is 23.0 days, not 22.0.*

## Analysis

**Supplier B.** B's lead times fall into two clusters, with no values in between:
- one cluster at 17–19 days;
- another at 28–31 days.

Every order in the second cluster breaches the 26-day cover. The long deliveries came at orders 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11, which looks like a recurring, systematic pattern rather than bad luck. Nothing suggests it will stop. On this record, roughly two in every five B orders would halt the line.

**Supplier A.** Eleven of A's 12 deliveries took 20–24 days, which leaves at least 2 days' margin inside the cover. The single exception was the 45-day delivery shipped during the three-week national port strike. That strike delayed all sea freight that month, has not recurred, and none is planned. This was an external, one-off event, not evidence of how A normally performs.

**Why the draft's reasoning misled.** The draft relied on three measures, and each pointed the wrong way:
- **Average lead time.** B's average looks fine because its fast deliveries offset its slow ones. The line, however, stops on each slow delivery.
- **Worst case.** Comparing worst cases favoured B only because A's worst case was the strike.
- **Range.** The wider spread for A comes entirely from that same single strike-affected order.

## Price

B is 5p per unit cheaper (£4.05 against £4.10, about 1.2%). On roughly 40,000 units a year, that saves about £2,000 annually. Set against roughly five line stoppages per twelve orders, this saving is immaterial unless a stoppage costs very little, which is unlikely for a halted assembly line.

## Quality

Both suppliers meet the K-220 specification, so quality does not separate them.

## Risks and caveats

- **Strike exposure.** A depends on sea freight and remains exposed to port disruption. A recurrence is possible, but on current evidence it is rare and usually announced in advance. Mitigation: keep B qualified as a back-up, and temporarily raise safety stock or switch orders to B when port disruption is signalled.
- **Small sample.** Twelve orders per supplier is limited evidence. Even so, a contrast of five exceedances against one (and that one explained) is large.
- **B could improve.** If B can identify and fix the cause of its 28–31-day deliveries, it could become competitive. The alternative is to raise safety stock to cover about 32 days, but holding more inventory has its own cost. Either option would be worth revisiting at the next review.

## Scope

This decision applies to K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts, with different specifications, volumes and routes. This data says nothing about which supplier suits them, so the draft's proposal to consolidate other components with B should be dropped.

## Recommendation

1. Award the K-220 contract to **Supplier A**.
2. Review lead-time performance quarterly, tracking the number of deliveries over 26 days rather than the average.
3. Keep **Supplier B** as a qualified back-up, particularly for any period of known port disruption.
4. Ask B to explain its recurring 28–31-day deliveries, so it can be reconsidered if it resolves them.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review: K-220 Supplier Analysis

**The analysis is sound, and the recommendation of Supplier A follows from the data.** All the figures check out, the decision criterion is right, and the scope is kept to K-220. I found only minor issues, none of which changes the conclusion.

## Figures checked

| Claim | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A mean 24.0 | 288 / 12 = 24.0 | ✓ |
| A median 22 | 6th and 7th sorted values are 22, 22 | ✓ |
| A mean excl. strike 22.1, max 24 | 243 / 11 = 22.09 | ✓ |
| B mean 23.0 (corrected from 22.0) | 276 / 12 = 23.0 | ✓ |
| B median 19 | 6th and 7th sorted values are 19, 19 | ✓ |
| B over 26 days: 5 of 12, at orders 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 | 30, 29, 31, 28, 30 | ✓ |
| B has no values between 19 and 28 | Gap confirmed | ✓ |
| A margin of at least 2 days (excl. strike) | Max 24 vs 26 | ✓ |
| Saving about £2,000/yr, about 1.2% | £0.05 × 40,000; 0.05 / 4.10 = 1.22% | ✓ |

## What it gets right

- **Criterion.** It uses the number of deliveries over 26 days, not the average, which is the right measure when every breach stops the line.
- **Strike order.** It explains why the 45-day delivery is excluded, keeps it visible in the table, and still lists strike exposure as a risk instead of dismissing it.
- **Scope.** It correctly drops the draft's proposal to consolidate other components with B. The data cannot support that.
- **Price.** The comparison is proportionate. £2,000 a year is small next to repeated line stoppages.

## Minor issues to fix

1. **Unsupported claim about strikes.** "It is rare and usually announced in advance" goes beyond the data, which says only that there has been no strike since and none is planned. Rephrase to something like "none has occurred since and none is planned," or cite a source.

2. **"Systematic pattern" is stated too strongly.** B's long deliveries fall exactly on alternate orders (3, 5, 7, 9, 11). That is a useful clue, perhaps alternating routes, carriers or depots. But with 12 orders it is still an inference. Saying "suggests a recurring cause" is safer. The strict alternation is also worth naming in recommendation 4, because it gives B a specific question to answer.

3. **References to "the draft."** The correction note and the "Why the draft's reasoning misled" section assume the reader has seen the earlier version. If this will circulate on its own, either summarise what the draft concluded (B, based on mean, worst case and range) or move the correction note to a footnote or change log.

4. **Small-sample point (optional).** The caveat could be made more concrete. Even allowing for sampling uncertainty, 0 breaches in 11 normal A orders against 5 in 12 for B is a clear difference. One sentence would do.

5. **Stoppage cost (optional).** The price argument says a stoppage costing "very little" is unlikely. A break-even figure would make this firmer: £2,000 a year spread over about 5 stoppages per 12 orders means B only wins if each stoppage costs less than a few hundred pounds. The exact number depends on order frequency, which isn't given.

## Verdict

**Approve with minor edits.** The numbers are correct, the reasoning holds, and Supplier A is the right choice for K-220. Fix item 1 before circulating. Items 2 and 3 are worth doing, and items 4 and 5 are optional.
</review>

# Receipt

**Overall verdict.** The review approves the analysis. It confirms that every figure is correct, that the 26-day exceedance criterion is the right one, and that Supplier A is the right choice. Nothing it raises changes the recommendation; the points below only change wording, framing and supporting detail.

I re-checked the figures: A's total is 288 (mean 24.0), or 243 excluding the strike order (mean 22.1). B's total is 276 (mean 23.0). Both medians are correct, and B's long deliveries fall at orders 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11.

1. **Unsupported claim about strikes (must fix).** The analysis says port strikes are "rare and usually announced in advance." The data only says there has been no strike since and none is planned. *Change:* limit the claim to what the notes state.

2. **"Systematic" is too strong.** Five long deliveries in 12 orders suggests a recurring cause but doesn't prove one. The strict alternation (every other order from order 3) is a useful clue, possibly alternating routes, carriers or depots. *Change:* soften the wording to "suggests a recurring cause," and put the alternation to B as a specific question in the recommendations.

3. **References to "the draft."** The correction note and the "Why the draft's reasoning misled" section assume the reader saw an earlier version. *Change:* make the document self-contained. Briefly state what the earlier reasoning concluded and why, and move the B-mean correction to a change note.

4. **Small sample (optional).** *Change:* make the caveat concrete. Even with only 12 orders each, 0 breaches in 11 normal A orders against 5 in 12 for B is a clear difference. I've added a significance test: Fisher's exact test, one-sided, p ≈ 0.02.

5. **Stoppage cost (optional).** *Change:* replace "a stoppage is unlikely to cost very little" with a break-even figure. The review's "a few hundred pounds" only holds if the firm orders about monthly. Order frequency isn't given, so I've shown the figure as depending on it: about £400 per stoppage at 12 orders a year, and about £90 at weekly ordering.

---

# Supplier Choice for K-220: Lead-Time Analysis

**Recommendation: award the K-220 contract to Supplier A.** Safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days, so the question is how often each supplier goes past 26 days.

- **Supplier B** went past 26 days in 5 of its last 12 orders, spread through the year.
- **Supplier A** went past it once, during a documented national port strike that has not recurred.

B's 5p unit saving, about £2,000 a year, would only pay off if a line stoppage cost very little.

## Decision criterion

A delivery over 26 days causes a stockout and halts the assembly line. The right measure is therefore **how often deliveries exceed 26 days**, and whether those exceedances are likely to recur.

Average lead time is a poor guide here, for two reasons:
- A supplier can have a good average and still breach the threshold often.
- A supplier with a slightly worse average can breach it almost never.

## Data

These are the last 12 orders from each supplier, in days from order placed to goods received, in date order.

- **Supplier A (sea):** 21, 23, 22, 24, 20, 22, **45**, 23, 21, 22, 24, 21
- **Supplier B (road/rail):** 18, 19, **30**, 17, **29**, 18, **31**, 19, **28**, 18, **30**, 19

Bold values exceed 26 days.

| | Supplier A | Supplier B |
|---|---|---|
| Mean lead time | 24.0 days | 23.0 days |
| Median lead time | 22 days | 19 days |
| Range | 20–45 days | 17–31 days |
| Orders over 26 days | **1 of 12** | **5 of 12 (42%)** |
| Cause of exceedances | February national port strike (documented, not recurred) | No identified disruption; spread through the year |
| Mean excluding A's strike order | 22.1 days (max 24) | n/a |

## Analysis

**Supplier B.** B's lead times fall into two separate clusters, with nothing between 19 and 28 days:
- one cluster at 17–19 days;
- another at 28–31 days.

Every order in the slow cluster breaches the 26-day cover. The slow deliveries fall exactly on alternate orders (3, 5, 7, 9 and 11). This regularity suggests a recurring cause, such as alternating routes, carriers or depots, rather than random delay. With 12 orders this is an inference, not proof, but nothing in the data suggests the pattern will stop. On this record, roughly two in five B orders would halt the line.

**Supplier A.** Eleven of A's 12 deliveries took 20–24 days, leaving at least 2 days' margin inside the cover. The single exception was the 45-day delivery shipped during the three-week national port strike, which delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since, and none is planned. The strike was an external event, not evidence of how A normally performs.

**Why the simpler measures point the wrong way.** On mean lead time, worst case and range, B looks better. Each of these is misleading here:
- **Mean.** B's fast deliveries offset its slow ones in the average. The line, however, stops on every slow delivery.
- **Worst case and range.** A looks worse only because of the single strike-affected order. Without it, A's worst case is 24 days.

**Is the difference just chance?** Twelve orders per supplier is a small sample. Even so, A had 0 breaches in 11 normal orders, against B's 5 in 12. A split that lopsided would be unlikely if the two suppliers really had the same breach rate (Fisher's exact test, one-sided, p ≈ 0.02).

## Price

B is 5p per unit cheaper: £4.05 against £4.10, about 1.2%. On roughly 40,000 units a year, that saves about £2,000 annually.

For B to come out ahead, that £2,000 must exceed the cost of its extra stoppages. Taking B's record as roughly 5 stoppages per 12 orders, the break-even cost per stoppage depends on how often the firm orders:

| Orders per year | Expected B stoppages per year | B wins only if each stoppage costs less than |
|---|---|---|
| 12 (monthly) | about 5 | about £400 |
| 52 (weekly) | about 22 | about £90 |

Order frequency isn't given, so treat these as illustrative. Halting an assembly line almost certainly costs more than either threshold.

## Quality

Both suppliers meet the K-220 specification, so quality does not separate them.

## Risks and caveats

- **Strike exposure.** A depends on sea freight and remains exposed to port disruption. There has been no strike since February and none is planned, but a future one cannot be ruled out. *Mitigation:* keep B qualified as a back-up, and raise safety stock or switch orders to B whenever port disruption is signalled.
- **Small sample.** Twelve orders each is limited evidence. The difference is nonetheless large and unlikely to be chance (see above). Quarterly monitoring will show whether it holds.
- **B could improve.** If B can find and fix the cause of its 28–31-day deliveries, it could become competitive. The other way to make B workable is to raise safety stock to cover about 32 days, but holding more inventory has its own cost. Both options are worth revisiting at the next review.

## Scope

This decision applies to K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts, with different specifications, volumes and routes. This data says nothing about which supplier suits them, so it should not be used to consolidate other components with either supplier.

## Recommendation

1. Award the K-220 contract to **Supplier A**.
2. Review lead-time performance quarterly, tracking the **number of deliveries over 26 days**, not the average.
3. Keep **Supplier B** as a qualified back-up, particularly for any period of known port disruption.
4. Ask B why its slow deliveries fall on alternate orders (3, 5, 7, 9, 11), and whether this reflects alternating routes, carriers or depots. Reconsider B if it resolves the cause.

---

*Change note: an earlier version gave B's mean as 22.0 days. The correct figure is 23.0 days (276 ÷ 12). That version also recommended B, based on mean lead time, worst case and range, and proposed consolidating other components with B. Both have been withdrawn for the reasons set out above.*
